report.headline: Every part is answered, but 2 serious problems cost you credit.
report.summary: You correctly identified the legal distinction regarding enforceability and the judicial need for harmony between the two concepts. However, the answer loses credit because it incorrectly limits the scope of Article 31C and fails to discuss the complementary nature of rights and principles. You should first clarify that Article 31C protects laws for all principles in Part IV and add a point on how they work together to achieve a welfare state.

report.question: Discuss the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy. (Answer in 150 words)

directives.meaning: Look at the issue from more than one side, with reasons, and reach a balanced view.

sentences.text: Fundamental Rights in Part III can be enforced in courts, while Article 37 says the Directive Principles in Part IV cannot be enforced by any court.
In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court held that the Directive Principles must yield to the Fundamental Rights.
The First Amendment then allowed special provisions for backward classes.
In Golaknath (1967) the Court held that Parliament could not amend the Fundamental Rights.
The Twenty-fifth Amendment added Article 31C to protect laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c).
In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Court upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the clause that barred judicial review.
The right to education in Article 21A began as a Directive Principle in Article 45.
The Forty-second Amendment extended Article 31C to all the Directive Principles, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension.
